lessons.title: Find evidence about your strengths
lessons.goal: Distinguish interests, demonstrated skills, and work values, then use evidence rather than a label to explore options.
lessons.opening: Jordan likes drawing and is often asked to organize group work. A friend says, ‘You should be a graphic designer.’ Is that enough information to choose a pathway?

teach.heading: Three different clues
teach.body: An interest is an activity that attracts your attention. A skill is something you can do, and stronger evidence comes from a specific task and result. A work value is a condition or purpose you care about, such as variety, stability, helping others, working outdoors, or flexible hours. Liking drawing does not prove that Jordan enjoys client deadlines; organizing a group does not prove a particular occupation is the only match.

teach.heading: Move from labels to examples
teach.body: Instead of writing ‘good communicator,’ name what you did: explained a complex idea to a younger student, checked whether they understood, and changed your example. That evidence can transfer to many roles. Ask what parts of the experience gave you energy and what was difficult. An interest inventory can suggest possibilities, but its results are questions to investigate, not instructions about your future.

teach.heading: Test a first hypothesis
teach.body: Make a short list of possible roles, including one outside your first idea. For each, compare actual day-to-day tasks, training, work conditions, and location. A provisional career hypothesis might say, ‘I want to explore jobs that combine visual problem solving with explaining ideas.’ It remains open to change after you read profiles, meet course requirements, or try a simulated task.

teach.heading: Check the quality of your evidence
teach.body: A useful evidence note has a context, an action, and an observable result. “I organized people well” is difficult to test; “I asked each group member what they could finish, put the tasks on a shared checklist, and noticed one deadline was at risk” gives a reader something concrete. Then add a boundary: the event involved classmates and one deadline, so it does not prove the learner will enjoy managing a large team. Strong reflection includes what was hard and what support helped, not only praise.

teach.heading: Look for patterns without turning them into labels
teach.body: One example can suggest a question; several examples across different settings can suggest a pattern. If someone enjoys explaining a science demonstration and helping a younger cousin with a game, the shared clue may be adapting explanations, not “must become a teacher.” Ask what part of each task was satisfying, what conditions mattered, and whether the skill appeared again. A quiet learner can show communication through careful writing or listening; evidence does not need to look like public speaking. Use the pattern to choose a next experiment, such as comparing two roles’ daily tasks.

document.title: Jordan’s evidence notes
rows: Enjoyed visual layout and revised after feedback
Enjoys every design job or client deadline
Wants to supervise people full time
document.note: These are fictional observations. A skill claim is stronger when it names the task, action, and result.

worked.prompt: Is ‘Jordan is creative’ strong career evidence?
steps: Locate an observable action: Jordan redesigned a poster after feedback.
Describe the specific skill: selecting and arranging information for an audience.
List an unanswered question: would Jordan enjoy similar tasks under real workplace constraints?
worked.conclusion: A general label becomes useful when it is tied to a task and a question to investigate.

worked.prompt: A quiz lists health care first, but Jordan is uneasy with direct patient care.
steps: Treat the quiz as a suggestion, not a verdict.
Explore different health roles and the actual duties in each.
Keep roles with suitable tasks; remove roles that conflict with a strong work preference.
worked.conclusion: One broad cluster can contain very different daily work.

practice.prompt: Which statement is the strongest evidence of a transferable skill?
choices: I am a leader
I chaired two meetings, shared tasks, and met our deadline
A quiz says I should lead
My friends say I am talented
feedback: This is a label without an observable action.
Yes. It names actions and a result that someone could discuss or verify.
A quiz result suggests a question; it is not evidence of performance.
Other people’s opinions can help, but ask for a concrete example.

practice.prompt: Jordan enjoys art but wants predictable hours. What should be researched next?
choices: Only job titles containing ‘artist’
Actual duties and schedules in two related occupations
One salary number without a date
Whether a friend approves
feedback: Titles alone hide important differences in work conditions.
Yes. Compare tasks and conditions against both the interest and the value.
Pay matters, but it does not answer the hours question.
A friend can offer ideas, not make the decision.

practice.prompt: How should an interest survey result be used?
choices: As a final career assignment
As proof that other careers are impossible
As a starting hypothesis to test with occupation evidence
As a replacement for course planning
feedback: Surveys cannot choose a career for a person.
A result cannot rule out every other pathway.
Yes. Compare suggestions with duties, training, conditions, and your own evidence.
You still need to check program requirements and options.

practice.prompt: Which note adds the most useful boundary to a skill claim?
choices: “I am naturally good at leadership.”
“In one three-person class project, I set check-ins; I still need to test whether I enjoy doing that repeatedly.”
“My friend says I should lead.”
“Leadership is a high-demand skill.”
feedback: This is a broad label without a task or limit.
Correct: it names context, action, and what remains untested.
Another person’s opinion is not direct evidence of task fit.
A broad labour claim does not show this learner’s experience.

practice.prompt: Two unrelated activities both involved explaining steps clearly. What is a careful inference?
choices: The learner must choose teaching as a career.
Adapting explanations may be a pattern worth exploring in more tasks.
The learner has proven expertise in every communication role.
The activities are irrelevant because they were unpaid.
feedback: Two examples do not dictate a single career.
Correct: the repeated action supports a hypothesis, not a verdict.
The evidence is narrow and cannot establish expertise across jobs.
Paid status is not required for transferable-skill evidence.

practice.prompt: A learner dislikes one part of an activity but likes another. What should the evidence record do?
choices: Hide the difficult part so the career idea looks stronger.
Name both the energizing task and the condition that made it difficult.
Discard the whole example as useless.
Treat discomfort as proof the whole occupation is unsuitable.
feedback: Selective evidence can distort the conclusion.
Correct: mixed evidence helps form better questions about work conditions.
An example can still show useful skills or preferences.
One activity is not equivalent to an entire occupation.

lessons.transfer: Amina likes repairing bicycles, explains repairs clearly, and dislikes long periods at a desk. Suggest two different roles to research and name the evidence and one missing fact for each.
lessons.evidence: Create a fictional or personal strengths card with two specific task examples, two work values, two pathways to explore, and one question that could change the plan.

lessons.title: Read an occupation profile like a researcher
lessons.goal: Use duties, working conditions and entry requirements to compare roles, and recognize what a profile cannot guarantee.
lessons.opening: Two job titles sound alike. One involves indoor design work; the other spends most days installing equipment at customer sites. Which details would tell you which actually fits?

teach.heading: Start with work, not a title
teach.body: Career clusters group related work, but a broad label can hide major differences. An occupation profile can describe main duties, conditions, education, certifications, skills, and typical pay. Read the daily activities first: what would you spend a Tuesday doing? Then identify the entry requirement and whether it is legally required, commonly preferred, or one of several routes. The distinction affects the time and cost of a plan.

teach.heading: Compare sources with dates
teach.body: A provincial profile summarizes an occupation across workplaces; a job posting describes one employer’s current opening. The two can differ without either being wrong. Record the profile’s source, region, and update date. A wage range does not promise that a new worker will receive the midpoint. A posting that asks for experience may be one route rather than the only route into the occupation.

teach.heading: Investigate the gaps
teach.body: Use a profile to draft questions. Does the work require travel or shift work? Is a licence needed in Alberta? Does training need to be renewed? What related roles use the same skills? Compare at least two roles and identify what you cannot settle from the profile alone. Later, you can use program pages and current postings to test the picture.

teach.heading: Separate typical work from entry requirements
teach.body: Profiles often combine tasks that occur frequently with requirements that apply only to some employers or specialties. Mark each statement as “typical task,” “legal or credential requirement,” “common preference,” or “one posting’s condition.” If the profile says a credential is required for a regulated occupation, verify that claim on the relevant Alberta regulator’s current page. If one employer prefers experience, that does not automatically make it a universal entry rule. A profile helps you build a research trail; it cannot replace checking the current rules attached to a specific role.

teach.heading: Use source disagreement as a question
teach.body: When two profiles disagree, compare the occupation name and code, region, update date, and the question each source answers. A national page might summarize a broad occupation, while an Alberta employer lists a narrow specialty. Do not average the statements or choose the one that sounds more encouraging. Record the conflict and identify a source closer to the decision, such as an official regulator for licensing or the program provider for admissions. If no authoritative answer appears, write “not yet verified” and ask an advisor before paying for training.

document.title: Two fictional profile cards
rows: Install and test equipment on site
Safety training and licence may be required
How much travel is typical locally?
document.note: These cards are invented for analysis; use current alis profiles for real occupations.

worked.prompt: Jordan likes visual problem solving but wants limited travel. Which role is a better first hypothesis?
steps: Compare the task and condition rows instead of relying on the similar titles.
Role A aligns with visual file preparation and less travel.
Keep the hypothesis provisional because the profile does not state actual employer schedules.
worked.conclusion: A reasonable first choice identifies both supporting evidence and an unresolved question.

worked.prompt: One current posting disagrees with a provincial profile about a certificate.
steps: Check whether the certificate is mandatory by law or preferred by one employer.
Check both source dates and regions.
Record the difference and verify with the program or regulator before changing a school plan.
worked.conclusion: One posting does not redefine every route into an occupation.

practice.prompt: Which profile section best answers ‘what would I do each day?’
choices: Duties and tasks
The occupation title
A single wage figure
The site logo
feedback: Yes. Tasks reveal what the work involves.
A title can conceal very different duties.
Pay does not describe daily work.
The logo identifies a source, not the duties.

practice.prompt: A wage range is shown for Alberta. What can you conclude?
choices: Every new worker receives the midpoint
The range describes reported pay, subject to source and context
The amount will be identical next year
Training is unnecessary
feedback: Starting pay may differ greatly.
Yes. Keep the region, date and definition with the number.
Wages and methods can change.
Pay data does not establish entry requirements.

practice.prompt: A posting asks for a certificate absent from a broad profile. What should you do?
choices: Ignore the posting
Assume the profile is fraudulent
Check whether the certificate is mandatory or employer-preferred
Abandon the pathway
feedback: A real employer may have a specific need.
Different scope or timing can explain the difference.
Yes. This resolves a planning-relevant distinction.
One difference is a research question, not a verdict.

practice.prompt: A job profile calls a certificate “usually preferred.” A regulator page names a mandatory credential for a protected title. What should the learner do?
choices: Treat the phrases as interchangeable.
Verify the exact role and follow the current regulator requirement for the protected title.
Ignore both and rely on a social post.
Assume all jobs in the cluster require that credential.
feedback: Preferred and legally required do not mean the same thing.
Correct: confirm the exact title and use the relevant regulator for a legal requirement.
A social post is not an authoritative credential source.
One title’s requirement may not apply to every role in a broad cluster.

practice.prompt: Two sources give different training lengths. Which comparison is most informative?
choices: Compare their dates, program scope, and whether one describes full-time or part-time study.
Choose the shorter number.
Add the numbers and divide by two.
Assume the source with more pictures is newer.
feedback: Correct: scope and study mode can explain a real difference.
The shortest figure may describe a different route.
Averaging unlike programs creates a number supported by neither.
Visual design does not establish a publication date.

practice.prompt: A learner sees one employer preference in a current posting. What conclusion is justified?
choices: Every employer requires it.
It is evidence about this opening; check other postings and official requirements before generalizing.
It is legally mandatory.
No one can enter the occupation without it.
feedback: One opening cannot establish a universal rule.
Correct: preserve the scope of the evidence and continue comparing.
A posting does not itself establish a legal requirement.
The claim exceeds the evidence from one employer.

lessons.transfer: A rural student finds a provincial profile for an occupation but no nearby postings this month. Explain two possible interpretations and two additional sources to check.
lessons.evidence: Build a two-occupation comparison using current alis profiles: cite duties, conditions, entry route, date, and one unresolved question for each.

lessons.title: Compare routes into a career
lessons.goal: Compare more than one education or training pathway using prerequisites, cost, time, credential and flexibility.
lessons.opening: Leah wants work involving electrical systems. A paid apprenticeship and a longer school route both sound possible. Which comparison would help without pretending one route is best for everyone?

teach.heading: Work backward from the destination
teach.body: Start with the exact role and confirm its real entry requirements. Some roles require a regulated credential; others accept different combinations of courses, work experience, portfolios, certificates or degrees. A college program, apprenticeship, direct employment and entrepreneurial route can lead to related work but not necessarily the same licence. Check the current program and regulator pages rather than relying on a friend’s memory.

teach.heading: Calculate the whole route
teach.body: Tuition is only one cost. Include tools, fees, transport, housing, time without full earnings, and any paid training. Compare what is known and label uncertain estimates. For example, a $2,000 fee with $1,200 travel costs is $3,200 in direct costs; it says nothing yet about income during the program. A lower up-front cost may still take longer, and a faster route may be less flexible if the learner later changes goals.

teach.heading: Keep alternatives live
teach.body: Make a primary route and a backup route. Record prerequisites to verify, a question for a school counsellor or program advisor, and a date to revisit the choice. A route map is useful when it can change with new evidence. It should not lock a student into a plan based on invented earnings or an unverified admission rule.

teach.heading: Compare more than the first payment
teach.body: A route comparison should identify when each cost occurs and which items are estimates. Up-front tuition, required equipment, application fees, transportation, housing, and time away from paid work can affect different learners differently. Keep one-time and recurring costs separate; a $400 tool purchase and $40 monthly travel cost cannot be compared by simply adding them without choosing a time period. Identify scholarships or paid training only when a current, eligible source supports them. If financing is needed, make borrowing a separate decision with its own total-cost and repayment analysis.

teach.heading: Check whether the routes reach the same destination
teach.body: Two programs may share a subject but lead to different credentials or scopes of practice. Trace the chain: program completion, any exam or supervised hours, registration or licence, then the actual job title. Ask the regulator or program provider which parts are mandatory, whether prior learning counts, and what happens if a learner pauses. Draw a decision point where evidence could change the plan. This protects a student from comparing one route’s introductory certificate with another route’s full qualification as if they were interchangeable.

document.title: Leah’s route sketch — fictional figures
rows: Paid work plus required training blocks
document.note: These figures and routes are teaching examples, not current program prices or credential rules.

worked.prompt: What are the stated direct costs?
steps: The $1,900 difference covers only listed costs, not earnings, living costs or future opportunity.
worked.conclusion: A calculation is useful only when its scope is explicit.

worked.prompt: Leah chooses Route A only because its direct cost is lower.
steps: Ask whether Route A actually grants access to the desired regulated role.
Check whether paid placements are available in Leah’s region.
Compare time, support needs and a backup if an employer place is unavailable.
worked.conclusion: Cost alone cannot establish pathway fit.

practice.prompt: Which cost is missing from tuition-only comparisons?
choices: Travel and required tools
A nickname for the program
The school’s logo
A friend’s preference
feedback: Yes. Direct and opportunity costs can extend beyond tuition.
The nickname does not affect the cost.
Branding is not a route cost.
Preference matters to the friend, but not as a cost figure.

practice.prompt: Route A costs $2,000 plus $1,200 travel. What is its stated direct cost?
feedback: Subtracting would not total the two expenses.
That is Route B’s stated direct cost.
That includes travel only.

practice.prompt: Which question must be answered before claiming the routes lead to the same role?
choices: Which brochure is brighter?
Who likes the teacher more?
Do both routes meet the current credential requirement?
Which is mentioned first online?
feedback: Design does not establish eligibility.
Personal liking does not prove credential status.
Yes. Check the current program and regulator requirements.
Search order is not evidence of equivalence.

practice.prompt: Route A lists $1,800 tuition, $250 tools, and $45 monthly transit for 10 months. What is the listed first-year total?
feedback: $2,050 omits all transit.
$2,095 includes only one transit month.
This does not follow the stated categories; use ten monthly costs.

practice.prompt: What makes an “alternate route” comparison fair?
choices: It leads to a related field, so the credential details do not matter.
Compare the actual title, credential, time, conditions, and additional steps each route requires.
Compare only which route has the lowest tuition.
Use a friend’s experience as the full program description.
feedback: Related work does not prove identical qualification or scope.
Correct: compare the destination and all route conditions.
Tuition alone omits time and other costs.
One person’s experience is useful context, not a complete official description.

practice.prompt: A program page and regulator page appear to conflict about entry. What is the strongest next step?
choices: Pay the application fee before asking.
Send the exact role and credential question to the program and regulator; record their current answers.
Assume the program page overrides all licensing rules.
Choose whichever answer supports the original plan.
feedback: Paying before resolving a key requirement risks avoidable cost.
Correct: ask the authorities responsible for the program and regulated title.
Program admissions and professional licensing are distinct.
Confirmation bias does not resolve the conflict.

lessons.transfer: A new route has lower fees but requires moving. Add housing, travel and lost earnings as known or unknown categories; explain what would change your recommendation.
lessons.evidence: Use the pathway comparison to defend a primary and backup route, with current sources for admission and credential facts.

lessons.title: Question a labour-market claim
lessons.goal: Interpret labour-market evidence by occupation, measure, place and date without treating a forecast as a promise.
lessons.opening: One report describes a growing occupation across Alberta. A search near Noor’s home finds two openings. Should Noor abandon the pathway or plan to move?

teach.heading: Name what was measured
teach.body: Labour-market sources may report employment, vacancies, wages, projections, or employer expectations. Those are different measures. A provincial forecast can describe a multi-year pattern while a job search shows advertised openings on one day. Neither directly predicts whether Noor will be hired after training. Write the measure, occupation definition, region, date, and source next to every figure so a reader can judge its relevance.

teach.heading: Compare like with like
teach.body: A wage range for experienced workers should not be presented as a starting wage. A province-wide shortage does not prove that jobs are available in one town. Before comparing two reports, check whether they cover the same occupation code, geography and time period. A small number of current postings may reflect a seasonal hiring cycle, an employer that recruits another way, or a genuinely limited local market.

teach.heading: Use uncertainty to plan
teach.body: The right result is usually a conditional plan. Noor can explore nearby related roles, check training and travel costs, look for recent postings over time, and ask what work is available locally. If moving is a possible option, it belongs alongside housing, support and lifestyle costs. Record what evidence would change the plan instead of labelling a pathway safe or unsafe from one graph.

teach.heading: Read the axis before the trend
teach.body: Before describing a graph, read the title, units, category, time window, and geographic coverage. A rising bar could represent a count, a percentage, or a forecast score; those do not mean the same thing. Check whether the vertical axis begins at zero and whether categories use matching definitions. If a report combines several years, note that it is not a current vacancy count. Copy the source name and retrieval date into your research notes so the claim can be checked later.

teach.heading: Triangulate without pretending to predict
teach.body: A second source is useful when it adds a different kind of evidence: current local postings, a provincial outlook, or an occupational profile. More sources do not automatically mean stronger evidence if all repeat the same old estimate. If one report suggests growth and current local postings are scarce, write both findings and consider season, region, commute, job title, and the date each was observed. Then state a conditional conclusion: “This is worth exploring if local opportunities and training costs remain workable.” Identify what new evidence would change that conclusion.

document.title: Two fictional pieces of labour-market evidence
rows: A modelled broad pattern; assumptions may change
Duties and reported ranges, not Noor’s offer
document.note: The records are invented to practise source interpretation; no real market figures are implied.

worked.prompt: The forecast is positive and the local search is small. Are the records inconsistent?
steps: Identify the first measure: a province-wide future model.
Identify the second measure: one day of local advertisements.
Explain how region, time and measure can produce different observations.
worked.conclusion: Both can be true; the comparison reveals a question to investigate.

worked.prompt: A classmate says Noor must move immediately.
steps: A current posting count does not describe the entire future training period.
Check related occupations, nearby regions and repeated observations.
Compare the cost and support implications of moving before recommending it.
worked.conclusion: A move is a conditional option, not an automatic conclusion.

practice.prompt: Which detail must travel with a wage figure?
choices: Its source, date, region and worker group
The colour of the website
A friend’s guessed salary
Only the highest number
feedback: Yes. These details determine what the figure actually describes.
Visual design does not define a statistic.
A guess is not a documented figure.
The high endpoint alone is misleading.

practice.prompt: A five-year provincial forecast and today’s local postings differ. What is the best explanation?
choices: One must be fabricated
They measure different places and time periods
No one can work locally
The forecast guarantees a job
feedback: A difference does not by itself prove fabrication.
Yes. Check measures and definitions before judging consistency.
A single search cannot establish that.
Forecasts are conditional, not guarantees.

practice.prompt: What would make a relocation decision stronger?
choices: The first search result only
The provincial average wage only
Repeated local evidence plus training, housing and support costs
A confident guess
feedback: One search is a narrow snapshot.
Wages alone omit costs and fit.
Yes. The decision needs multiple relevant pieces of evidence.
Confidence is not a substitute for source quality.

practice.prompt: A chart’s title says “projected openings,” but a learner calls the bars “jobs guaranteed to be available.” What was misread?
choices: A projection was treated as a promise of individual vacancies.
The learner included a citation.
The report’s region was recorded.
The axis units were included.
feedback: Correct: projected openings estimate a broader pattern; they do not guarantee a current opening for one person.
Citations help readers verify claims.
Region is important context, not an error.
Units help interpret a chart.

practice.prompt: A local search shows few postings over one week. What can the learner say?
choices: The occupation will disappear locally.
Few postings appeared in that search window; collect more evidence over time and check other channels.
The provincial forecast must be false.
No one is employed in the occupation.
feedback: One short search cannot establish future disappearance.
Correct: this is a scoped observation with a sensible next check.
Local postings and provincial forecasts measure different things.
A vacancy search does not count existing workers.

practice.prompt: Which evidence best supports a relocation question?
choices: A province-wide wage chart by itself.
A comparison of local openings, likely commute/housing costs, and relevant role requirements.
A friend’s guess about another city.
A national shortage label without a date.
feedback: A wage chart alone omits access and living costs.
Correct: it combines opportunity and practical constraints.
A guess is not verifiable evidence.
An undated label lacks context and may not match a location.

lessons.transfer: An urban student sees many advertised openings but also long training requirements. Explain why demand alone is not a complete pathway decision and name two further checks.
lessons.evidence: Annotate two real Alberta labour-market sources with measure, occupation, region, date, limit and the decision each can support.

lessons.title: Build a high-school route with checkpoints
lessons.goal: Use current prerequisites to draft a flexible high-school plan and identify decisions that need school guidance.
lessons.opening: Tariq wants to keep two different post-school routes possible, but the course choices appear to diverge next year. How can a plan preserve options without inventing admission rules?

teach.heading: Work from current requirements
teach.body: A high-school plan connects a possible destination to courses and experiences available now. Start with the current admission or entry page for each pathway. Record required courses separately from recommended preparation. Note grade thresholds and deadlines only when a current source states them, because they may change. Ask the school to confirm sequencing, availability and graduation requirements rather than assuming that a program page describes your timetable.

teach.heading: Find the shared steps
teach.body: Two routes often share foundational courses and skills. Place those common steps first, then mark a decision point where a specialized course or application is needed. If one course has a prerequisite, draw the chain: prerequisite, later course, program requirement. A chain reveals why delaying a course may close an option temporarily and where a summer, online or alternate route might exist if the school confirms it.

teach.heading: Make revision part of the plan
teach.body: Put a date and trigger on each checkpoint. A new interest, changed grade, updated program requirement or transport issue can justify revision. A useful backup route is a researched pathway, not ‘do something else.’ Keep a note of who can verify an uncertainty. This protects students from treating an early plan as an unchangeable promise.

teach.heading: Trace prerequisites as a sequence
teach.body: A prerequisite is not only a course name; it is a dependency that affects when a later option can be taken. Draw a simple chain with the source and school confirmation beside each step. If a course is unavailable in a planned term, ask about the next offering, approved equivalent, or alternate route before deleting a career goal. Keep graduation requirements distinct from a specific college admission requirement. A school timetable and a university program page answer different questions, and both may need current confirmation.

teach.heading: Build a checkpoint around a decision
teach.body: Each route can have a “continue, revise, or investigate” point. For example, after reviewing the official admission page and meeting a counsellor, the learner can confirm the course sequence or identify an unresolved conflict. Record the date, evidence checked, and who can verify the next uncertainty. Avoid turning a grade threshold into a personal worth judgement: a result is information for choosing support or a different sequence. A backup route is strongest when it shares useful preparation and has been researched, not when it is simply a vague fallback.

document.title: Tariq’s fictional pathway map
document.note: No listed course is a real admission requirement. Verify actual Alberta high-school and program rules before using a plan.

worked.prompt: A program page requires a course that Tariq cannot take until after a prerequisite.
steps: Place the prerequisite in an earlier term.
Check whether the later course is offered when needed.
Bring the sequence and a backup question to a school counsellor.
worked.conclusion: A program requirement becomes a timetable decision only after school availability is checked.

worked.prompt: Route B’s website changes its entry rule.
steps: Record the new source and date.
Identify which part of Tariq’s plan changes and which common steps remain useful.
Update the next checkpoint rather than discarding all earlier work.
worked.conclusion: A revisable plan saves the reasoning behind each choice.

practice.prompt: What is the strongest basis for a claimed prerequisite?
choices: A current program or regulator page
An old social post
A friend’s memory
The course with the most impressive title
feedback: Yes. Record the exact page and date, then confirm local course sequencing.
Requirements can change after a post.
Memory is a lead to verify, not a rule source.
A title does not establish admission eligibility.

practice.prompt: Two routes share a course. Where should it appear?
choices: Only on the favourite route
In the shared preparation before the decision point
Nowhere until graduation
As proof both careers are identical
feedback: The common step supports both options.
Yes. Shared preparation can keep alternatives open.
Delaying it could restrict sequencing.
A shared course does not make occupations identical.

practice.prompt: A learner cannot take a needed course at the planned time. What next?
choices: Assume admission is impossible forever
Invent an exemption
Ask the school and program about valid sequences or alternatives
Copy another student’s timetable
feedback: Other valid paths may exist.
Only the responsible institution can confirm an exception.
Yes. Verify what options are actually available.
Another student’s circumstances may differ.

practice.prompt: A student cannot access a required course in the planned semester. What is the strongest next step?
choices: Drop the pathway immediately.
Ask the school about later offerings, approved equivalents, and sequence effects before revising the route.
Assume an unrelated course will count.
Ignore the prerequisite.
feedback: A scheduling problem may have alternate solutions.
Correct: verify realistic school options and how timing affects later steps.
An equivalency requires confirmation.
Ignoring a dependency can delay eligibility.

practice.prompt: Why keep the source date in a high-school plan?
choices: Requirements, course offerings, and deadlines can change.
It makes a plan impossible to revise.
It proves admission is guaranteed.
It replaces checking with a counsellor.
feedback: Correct: a date helps identify when evidence may need refreshing.
Dated evidence makes revision easier, not harder.
A source date cannot promise admission.
School staff can confirm local sequencing and availability.

practice.prompt: Which is a useful checkpoint outcome?
choices: “I will see what happens.”
“After confirming the prerequisite and next course offering, I will keep, adjust, or research the route.”
“I must follow my first plan no matter what.”
“If I change the route, I failed.”
feedback: No decision trigger is defined.
Correct: this ties a decision to evidence and allows revision.
New evidence can justify a change.
Pathway revision is a normal planning skill.

lessons.transfer: A new program adds a portfolio requirement. Show where it belongs in a two-year plan, what support is needed, and when the plan should be reviewed.
lessons.evidence: Create a primary and backup high-school route with verified prerequisites, a decision date, and two questions for a teacher or counsellor.

lessons.title: Explore employment and entrepreneurship routes
lessons.goal: Compare employment and entrepreneurship as routes with different responsibilities, risks and evidence needs.
lessons.opening: Kai enjoys repairing bikes and has helped neighbours. Does that make a repair business the obvious next step, or is employment with a shop another useful route?

teach.heading: Separate skill from business viability
teach.body: Being skilled at a task is only one part of earning from it. An employee usually works within an organization’s systems; an entrepreneur also has to find customers, set prices, track costs, arrange safe work, manage records and accept income uncertainty. Neither route is automatically more independent or more secure. Kai should identify the responsibilities they want to learn and the ones they are not yet ready to take on.

teach.heading: Test a small opportunity
teach.body: An opportunity claim needs evidence: who has the problem, what solution they use now, what it costs to provide a safe alternative, and whether the price leaves enough after expenses. In a fictional trial, five repairs at $30 each produce $150 in revenue. If parts cost $75 and other costs are $25, $50 remains before other obligations. Revenue is not profit, and one week cannot establish steady demand.

teach.heading: Build an adaptable route
teach.body: Kai could learn in an established shop, continue a school enterprise exercise, or later test a small service under the appropriate rules and supervision. A plan should include skill development, customer evidence, safety and legal questions, start-up needs, and a fallback. Do not direct minors to solicit strangers or start a real business to complete an online lesson.

teach.heading: Test customer need before estimating income
teach.body: A small business idea begins with a problem, not a guessed sales total. Identify who experiences the problem, how often it occurs, how people handle it now, and what evidence would show that a proposed service is wanted. An online poll of friends may reveal interest but not whether people will pay a sustainable price. Use a fictional trial or supplied data in this course; students should not solicit strangers, collect customer data, or spend real money to earn credit.

teach.heading: Calculate contribution, not just sales
teach.body: Revenue is money received before costs. A simple contribution estimate subtracts direct costs, but it may still omit permits, insurance, equipment wear, payment fees, tax obligations, and unpaid time. If a fictional service earns $150 and listed materials and transport cost $62, the remaining $88 is not automatically personal income or profit. List which costs were included and which were not assessed. Check current rules and adult supervision before any real venture, especially where a learner is a minor or the work involves safety risks. Ask whether the customer could choose not to buy and what evidence would distinguish politeness from demand. A route remains a hypothesis until cost, safety, and repeat interest are checked.

document.title: Kai’s fictional one-week service test

worked.prompt: Kai says, ‘I made $150 profit.’
steps: Identify $150 as five payments received: revenue.
Subtract $75 parts and $25 other listed expenses.
State that $50 remains before unlisted costs and time.
worked.conclusion: Calling revenue profit hides the resources needed to provide the service.

worked.prompt: Kai chooses a shop job first.
steps: The job may provide training and exposure to customer needs.
Kai can observe which tasks they enjoy and what safety systems matter.
A later business idea can use that evidence without claiming employment is a failure.
worked.conclusion: Employment can be a deliberate learning route toward or alongside entrepreneurship.

practice.prompt: In Kai’s fictional test, what is $150?
choices: Revenue before costs
Profit after all costs
A guaranteed weekly wage
The cost of parts
feedback: Yes. It is the amount paid by customers before expenses.
Costs and time have not all been accounted for.
Customer demand could vary; it is not a wage guarantee.
Parts cost $75 in the case.

practice.prompt: What is the stated amount remaining after listed costs?
feedback: That ignores all costs.
That subtracts only one cost category.
That is one expense line.

practice.prompt: What would strengthen the business opportunity claim?
choices: A single excited comment
A bigger logo
Customer need, costs, safe delivery and repeated demand evidence
An assumption that repairs are always needed
feedback: One comment is a lead, not sustained evidence.
Branding does not prove viability.
Yes. Test the actual problem and costs across more than one case.
A broad claim does not establish customers or pricing.

feedback: $210 is revenue before costs.
$84 is the listed cost, not what remains.
This adds costs to revenue rather than subtracting them.

practice.prompt: What does a positive remainder after listed costs establish?
choices: That the business is guaranteed profitable.
Only that revenue exceeded the costs included in that calculation.
That customers will return.
That legal and safety checks are unnecessary.
feedback: Unlisted costs and demand remain unknown.
Correct: the conclusion must match the costs actually counted.
Repeat demand needs separate evidence.
Rules and safe-work questions still need checking.

practice.prompt: Which is the strongest low-risk way to test an idea for an online lesson?
choices: Have students approach strangers with a sales pitch.
Use fictional customer feedback and a supplied cost sheet to compare options.
Require a real purchase.
Publish a student’s home address to attract customers.
feedback: Stranger solicitation is unnecessary and may be unsafe.
Correct: a simulation teaches the reasoning without exposing students.
Real spending is not needed for course evidence.
Publishing location data creates privacy and safety risks.

lessons.transfer: A fictional student sells handmade items for $20 each, with $8 materials and $3 selling costs per item. Explain the remaining amount for four sales and two uncertainties before calling it a viable business.
lessons.evidence: Compare an employment route and an entrepreneurial route for the same interest, including responsibilities, evidence needed and a safe next learning step.

lessons.title: Balance a plan when life changes
lessons.goal: Revise a career plan when time, location, wellbeing or support changes without treating revision as failure.
lessons.opening: Maya’s plan assumes after-school travel twice a week. A family responsibility now takes that time. What should change first: the goal, the route, or the timing?

teach.heading: Plans use limited resources
teach.body: Time, energy, transport, money and support all affect a pathway. A school schedule that looks possible on paper may conflict with work or care responsibilities. Show the actual week rather than assuming that a student can ‘try harder.’ Identify fixed commitments and flexible blocks. A healthy plan includes sleep and recovery; constant overload is a signal to revise the plan, not proof of poor character.

teach.heading: Separate destination from route
teach.body: A changed situation does not always change what Maya values. They may keep the same long-term interest but choose a different course sequence, online learning option, local experience or later deadline. Conversely, new experience may show that the destination itself no longer fits. Explain which piece changed and why. A backup route should protect the important goal while fitting the new constraint.

teach.heading: Use a review trigger
teach.body: Write down what evidence will prompt another check: a course result, an application response, a work trial, a timetable change or a support conversation. Ask for help where a school or program decision is needed. A good revision records the old assumption, the new evidence, the change and the next test. This makes the plan useful across transitions rather than a single assignment.

teach.heading: Use a capacity check, not a perfect-week assumption
teach.body: A weekly plan should include travel time, setup, transitions, meals, rest, and tasks that do not happen at a fixed hour. Mark fixed commitments first, then estimate realistic flexible time. If the plan only works when every bus is on time and no assignment takes longer than expected, it has no buffer. A simple calendar can reveal a conflict before a student interprets it as a motivation problem. Keep any personal schedule private; the lesson can use the fictional week supplied in class.

teach.heading: Revise the constraint that changed
teach.body: When a new constraint appears, separate the goal, route, and schedule. If a bus route ends earlier, a learner may keep an interest in a field but choose a local course, different work hours, an online option, or a later experience. Compare consequences and ask the school to verify options that affect graduation or admission. A revision note should show the original assumption, the new evidence, the chosen change, and a date to check again. It should also name the support needed rather than implying that the learner must solve every barrier alone.

document.title: Maya’s fictional weekly planning board
rows: Could support local or online work
document.note: The board is a reasoning aid; no learner is asked to disclose their real family responsibilities.

worked.prompt: Maya’s goal still fits, but the Tuesday route does not.
steps: State the goal and the new time constraint separately.
Look for a feasible alternative: Thursday plus a local or online Saturday option, if available.
Confirm the option before treating it as part of the plan.
worked.conclusion: A route can change while the larger goal remains.

worked.prompt: A peer says Maya should fill every free hour with preparation.
steps: A calendar is not evidence of sustainable capacity.
Protect required commitments and recovery.
Adjust scope or timing and ask for support rather than hiding the overload.
worked.conclusion: A realistic plan includes wellbeing and cannot depend on exhaustion.

practice.prompt: Which revision best responds to a new travel constraint?
choices: Separate the goal from the route and test a feasible alternative
Declare the student unmotivated
Keep an impossible schedule
Delete every future option
feedback: Yes. Identify what changed and which alternative preserves the aim.
The constraint is practical evidence, not a character judgement.
An unusable schedule is not a plan.
One blocked route does not erase all options.

practice.prompt: What belongs in a plan review note?
choices: Only a new title
Old assumption, new evidence, change and next check
A promise never to change again
Only a grade
feedback: A title cannot explain the reasoning.
Yes. The record shows why the revision is justified.
Future information may require another revision.
A grade may be relevant but is not the full explanation.

practice.prompt: Why include recovery time?
choices: To make the table longer
To avoid all effort
Because a sustainable plan must fit human limits and other commitments
Because every student has identical capacity
feedback: Formatting is not the reason.
The plan still includes meaningful work.
Yes. Capacity and wellbeing affect whether a route is workable.
Needs differ across learners and situations.

practice.prompt: A plan has no travel or transition time and fills every evening. What is the clearest problem?
choices: It depends on a perfect week and leaves no usable buffer.
It proves the learner lacks commitment.
It will always work if the goal matters.
It should add more commitments.
feedback: Correct: omitted transition time makes the schedule fragile.
A plan constraint is not a character judgement.
Motivation does not remove travel or delays.
More commitments worsen an already full plan.

practice.prompt: A transit change makes the original route difficult. Which statement best separates goal from route?
choices: The learner must abandon the interest.
The learner can keep the interest and test a local, later, or online route with school confirmation.
The learner should ignore the transit change.
The original timetable is still valid without checking.
feedback: A transport constraint does not automatically invalidate the goal.
Correct: revise the means and verify feasibility.
Ignoring a known constraint weakens the plan.
Changed conditions call for a review.

practice.prompt: What belongs in a useful revision record?
choices: Only the new answer.
Old assumption, new evidence, change, reason, and next review point.
A statement that the first plan was perfect.
Private information about another family member.
feedback: Without the reason, the plan is hard to evaluate.
Correct: this creates a traceable decision and next step.
A plan can change when evidence changes.
Other people’s private details are not needed.

lessons.transfer: A fictional learner receives a new school timetable and can no longer attend a planned program visit. Revise the route without inventing program availability; name who could confirm an alternative.
lessons.evidence: Revise an earlier fictional or personal career plan: old assumption, new evidence, updated route, review date and one support request.

lessons.title: Check the rules before a first shift
lessons.goal: Use current Alberta sources to investigate a young worker’s hours, conditions and pay statement without guessing a legal rule.
lessons.opening: A fictional 15-year-old receives a late retail shift during the school term. A co-worker says that late hours are always allowed if a manager agrees. What should the student check?

teach.heading: Identify the worker and the work
teach.body: Employment rules can depend on age, industry, task, school hours and time of day. Begin a case file with those facts before looking up a rule. In Alberta, the youth employment page separates ages 13–14 from ages 15–17 and describes additional hour restrictions. Do not apply a rule from a different age group or province. For a real situation, consult the current official page and the school or workplace rather than a remembered number.

teach.heading: Read the written record
teach.body: A schedule shows planned work; a pay statement shows recorded work and deductions. Keep the two distinct. Compare dates, start and end times, breaks, duties and pay period. Ask whether the hours actually worked match the record. A pay rate or break rule should be checked against the current Alberta Employment Standards page and the worker’s agreement. One missing detail can change the conclusion.

teach.heading: Use a careful response
teach.body: If a shift appears to conflict with a rule, save the schedule, note the source and its date, and ask the employer for clarification in a specific, respectful way. A student can ask a trusted adult or school contact for help. A fictional lesson cannot resolve every employment arrangement; the skill is to locate the applicable rule, identify uncertainty and choose a safe next step.

teach.heading: Check the exact category and exception
teach.body: A youth work rule may apply differently depending on the worker’s age, the type of work, the industry, school attendance, and the time of day. Before applying a summary, write down those facts and compare them with the scope of the current Alberta rule. Some occupations or tasks can have additional restrictions or permits. Never assume that a rule described for a 15–17-year-old also applies to someone aged 13–14, or that permission from a supervisor overrides a legal restriction.

teach.heading: Separate a schedule concern from a pay concern
teach.body: A schedule shows expected hours; a time record and pay statement help establish what was recorded and paid. If they differ, first compare the same dates, breaks, and duties. Keep a copy of the record and ask a specific question, such as “The schedule shows 6–10 p.m., but the recorded end time is 9:30; can we check the closing log?” For a real concern, consult current Alberta Employment Standards guidance or a trusted adult. A lesson calculation is not a legal ruling. Age-specific exceptions and work permits may matter for particular tasks. When official guidance is unclear, preserve the schedule and ask Employment Standards or a trusted school contact before treating a shift as permitted.

Locate the 15–17 section on the current Alberta youth employment page.
Check the specific retail hour and supervision rules against the scheduled interval.
worked.conclusion: A plausible rule for a different case is not evidence for this worker.

worked.prompt: The posted schedule ends at midnight but the time record ends at 12:30 a.m.
steps: Keep copies of both records and note the dates.
Ask whether the later work was directed or recorded correctly.
Check the current rules and seek school or official help if the discrepancy remains.
worked.conclusion: Document the observed difference before claiming a violation or a payroll error.

practice.prompt: Which fact is needed before applying a youth employment rule?
choices: The worker’s age and type of work
The store’s favourite colour
The manager’s confidence
The longest shift anyone has ever worked
feedback: Yes. Age, work type, school time and hours can change the applicable rule.
Colour has no bearing on the rule.
Confidence cannot replace the governing source.
A different worker’s history does not define this case.

practice.prompt: Which record shows the hours that were actually entered for pay?
choices: An advertisement
A time record or pay statement
A career survey
A program brochure
feedback: An ad is unrelated to this work period.
Yes. Compare that record with the schedule and worker’s notes.
A survey does not document paid hours.
A brochure is not an employment record.

practice.prompt: A rule summary conflicts with the current Alberta page. What should guide the case?
choices: The older summary
The easiest sentence to remember
The current official source with its scope and date
The worker’s guess
feedback: An older summary may be out of date.
Ease of recall does not determine the rule.
Yes. Verify the official rule and whether it applies to the case.
A guess is a reason to research, not a conclusion.

practice.prompt: Which fact is especially important when checking a youth shift rule?
choices: Worker age and the actual work/time conditions.
The colour of the uniform.
How confident the supervisor sounds.
What a different province allows.
feedback: Correct: applicability can depend on age and work conditions.
Uniform colour does not determine the rule.
Confidence does not replace the applicable standard.
Rules in another jurisdiction may not apply in Alberta.

practice.prompt: A recorded time differs from the schedule. What is the best first evidence check?
choices: Compare the same date, actual hours and break record.
Assume the schedule is always the final pay record.
Assume the employer intentionally changed it.
Change the pay statement yourself.
feedback: Correct: align the relevant records before drawing a conclusion.
A schedule is planned time, not necessarily the hours entered for pay.
A discrepancy needs investigation, not an unsupported motive claim.
Workers should not alter employer records.

practice.prompt: A summary conflicts with a current official Alberta page. How should a student proceed?
choices: Use the older summary because it is shorter.
Check the official page’s scope/date and ask an appropriate adult or authority if unclear.
Average both rules.
Choose the rule that permits more hours.
feedback: A short summary may omit exceptions or be outdated.
Correct: verify applicability and seek help with unresolved details.
Rules are not averaged.
Convenience does not determine which rule applies.

lessons.transfer: A fictional 14-year-old is offered a different task at a restaurant. List the facts and official sources needed before saying whether the work is permitted.
lessons.evidence: Create a workplace case file with dates, age, setting, records, applicable current Alberta source, remaining uncertainty and a respectful help request.

lessons.title: Stop, identify and control a hazard
lessons.goal: Identify a hazard, use the three worker rights and choose a safe immediate and follow-up response.
lessons.opening: On a first shift, Devin is asked to use an unlabelled cleaning liquid beside a poorly ventilated storage area. A supervisor is busy. What happens before Devin uses it?

teach.heading: A hazard is a source of harm
teach.body: A hazard is not the same as an injury that has already happened. The unlabelled liquid creates uncertainty about exposure; the ventilation condition may increase risk. Before starting, identify what could go wrong, who could be affected and what information is missing. A worker should receive the information, instruction, training and supervision needed for the task. An instruction to ‘be careful’ does not identify the substance or safe procedure.

teach.heading: Use the three rights
teach.body: Canadian occupational health and safety guidance describes the rights to know about hazards, participate in health and safety decisions, and refuse work that may endanger someone. The right to know supports requesting the label, safety information and training before use. Participation includes reporting the concern and suggesting a safer method. If dangerous conditions remain, the worker should follow the applicable refusal process; the exact procedure belongs to the jurisdiction and workplace.

teach.heading: Control the risk and document
teach.body: Pause the task, keep others away from the uncertain exposure if safe to do so, and ask the supervisor for guidance and the correct procedure. Do not test an unknown chemical by smelling it or mixing it with another product. Record the concern through the workplace process and follow up. If an immediate serious danger exists, move to safety and use the emergency procedure. The lesson case is fictional; a real worker should use current Alberta guidance and workplace training.

teach.heading: Choose a control that removes or reduces exposure
teach.body: Risk control is strongest when it eliminates the hazard or separates people from it, rather than depending only on reminders to be careful. For the unknown cleaner in the case, a learner should not touch, smell, mix, or pour it. Keep people away if safe, report it, and wait for someone trained to identify and handle it. A glove or mask is not a substitute for knowing what the substance is and whether that equipment is appropriate.

teach.heading: Refusal is a process, not a dare
teach.body: The right to refuse dangerous work is not an invitation to take risks or to confront someone alone. Tell the supervisor promptly, explain the specific hazard, and follow the current workplace and Alberta OHS process. The supervisor may investigate and take corrective action; the worker should not resume until the concern is addressed through the process. If danger is immediate, leave the danger area and follow emergency directions. The exact legal process and any exceptions must be checked against current official guidance. Never trade a worker’s safety for speed or customer convenience. A safe stop should be communicated promptly so the workplace can protect others and arrange trained assistance.

document.note: The table shows a decision sequence, not a complete legal refusal procedure.

steps: Prior use does not identify the chemical or exposure risk.
Devin pauses and asks for the label, instructions and supervisor guidance.
The task resumes only when a safe procedure is established.
worked.conclusion: Anecdote is not hazard information.

worked.prompt: The supervisor supplies the correct label and training but ventilation is still inadequate.
steps: Reassess all hazards; solving one does not erase another.
Report the ventilation issue and seek a safe alternative.
Use the workplace and Alberta process if dangerous conditions remain.
worked.conclusion: Risk control is a sequence of decisions, not a single checkbox.

choices: Pause and request hazard information and training
Use a small amount to test it
Mix it with water without instructions
Keep working because someone else did
feedback: Yes. The substance and procedure must be identified before use.
Testing exposure can itself be harmful.
Mixing chemicals without instructions can increase danger.
Prior use does not establish safety.

practice.prompt: Reporting a hazard and suggesting a safer method uses which right?
choices: Only the right to be paid
The right to participate
A guarantee of no future risk
Permission to ignore a supervisor
feedback: Pay is a different workplace issue.
Yes. Workers can contribute to safety decisions and report concerns.
No method removes every risk automatically.
Participation uses a workplace process, not silence or defiance.

practice.prompt: The label is supplied but the room still lacks safe ventilation. What is the lesson?
choices: The hazard is gone
The worker must finish quickly
Reassess each remaining hazard before proceeding
Ventilation never matters
feedback: A label resolves only part of the uncertainty.
Speed does not control exposure.
Yes. Each relevant hazard needs a safe response.
Airflow can affect exposure risk.

practice.prompt: Why is “wear gloves” not enough for an unidentified liquid?
choices: The correct protective equipment depends on knowing the substance and task.
Gloves make all chemicals safe.
Personal protective equipment removes the liquid.
The worker should test it by touch first.
feedback: Correct: without identification, you cannot know whether the glove is suitable.
Gloves do not protect against every chemical or exposure route.
PPE may reduce exposure but does not remove the source.
Touching an unknown substance creates exposure.

practice.prompt: What makes a control stronger than a reminder to “be careful”?
choices: It removes the hazard or reliably separates people from it.
It blames the least experienced worker.
It hides the hazard from visitors.
It assumes an injury will not happen.
feedback: Correct: controls should reduce exposure at the source or by separation.
Blame does not control risk.
Hiding a hazard leaves it present.
Assumptions do not prevent harm.

practice.prompt: A worker has reported the hazard but it remains. What is an appropriate response?
choices: Follow the applicable refusal process and do not resume until addressed.
Return because the supervisor heard about it.
Ask a classmate to test the substance.
Mix it with water to identify it.
feedback: Correct: report and follow the safe-work process; hearing a report is not itself a control.
A report does not establish that the hazard is controlled.
Another inexperienced worker should not be exposed.
Mixing unknown substances can create additional danger.

lessons.transfer: A fictional worker is assigned a tool with a damaged guard. Apply the identify, pause, ask, report and reassess sequence; distinguish the right to know from the right to refuse.
lessons.evidence: Analyze a new Alberta workplace hazard case: identify sources of harm, use the three rights, and show immediate and follow-up actions with an official source.

lessons.title: Act on responsibilities and concerns
lessons.goal: Connect worker and employer responsibilities to a specific, documented workplace concern.
lessons.opening: A worker notices the closing checklist skips a machine inspection. They feel awkward raising it because the team is behind schedule. How could they act responsibly?

teach.heading: Responsibilities are shared
teach.body: A safe workplace requires more than one person following rules. Employers must provide systems, information and supervision required by applicable law; workers follow safe procedures, use provided protection correctly and report hazards. Saying ‘everyone is responsible’ does not mean a new worker must solve a hazardous system alone. In the case, the worker can stop a task they cannot do safely and ask how the inspection should be completed.

teach.heading: Make the concern specific
teach.body: A useful report names the task, observed condition, time and possible consequence. ‘The machine is dangerous’ is less actionable than ‘the guard was loose during the 4 p.m. closing check; I stopped using it and told the shift lead.’ Keep facts separate from assumptions about someone’s motives. Follow the workplace process and keep an appropriate record, without sharing private worker information publicly.

teach.heading: Escalate with purpose
teach.body: If the first conversation does not resolve a concern, use the next workplace contact or current Alberta occupational health and safety guidance. For wage or scheduling matters, the relevant employment-standards route may differ from a safety concern. Identify the issue before selecting an agency or complaint path. Asking a trusted adult, union representative where applicable, or school contact for help can support a young worker.

teach.heading: Choose the right reporting route for the issue
teach.body: A workplace can involve several distinct concerns: an immediate hazard, unpaid wages, schedule limits, harassment, or unsafe equipment. Start by naming the issue and its urgency. A safety concern belongs in the workplace OHS reporting process and may involve Alberta OHS guidance; a pay question may involve the employer’s payroll records and Employment Standards. Some situations need more than one route. Avoid sending a complaint to an agency that has no mandate for that issue, and seek a trusted adult’s help when uncertain.

teach.heading: Close the loop after reporting
teach.body: A report is more useful when it states what action is requested and how the worker will know whether the risk was addressed. For example, “Please confirm the guard is secured and show me the inspection procedure before I use the saw again.” Note the response and any change to the equipment or instruction. If the hazard persists, follow the escalation path rather than treating silence as resolution. Do not photograph coworkers or publish allegations online; preserve relevant records privately and use the workplace’s appropriate channels. Keep the report factual and limited to people who need to respond. A clear record helps identify whether a control changed and prevents the same hazard from being passed to the next shift.

rows: At 4 p.m. the guard was loose; I stopped the machine and told the shift lead
Time, observation and action can be checked
document.note: The details are fictional and use no personal or confidential information.

steps: Name the observed condition and when it happened.
State what work was paused or made safe.
Ask for the inspection or repair procedure and a response.
worked.conclusion: Specific records help the workplace act without inventing blame.

worked.prompt: A pay error is reported only to the safety contact.
steps: Identify that the issue concerns earnings records, not a machine hazard.
Find the payroll or employment-standards route.
Keep the pay-period evidence and request clarification from the appropriate person.
worked.conclusion: The correct help route depends on the type of concern.

practice.prompt: Which report is easiest to investigate?
choices: The guard was loose at 4 p.m.; I stopped using the machine
Everyone is careless
This always happens
Someone must be punished
feedback: Yes. It gives an observation, time and immediate action.
It assigns a broad motive without a specific event.
‘Always’ needs evidence and dates.
Punishment is not the first factual description of the hazard.

practice.prompt: Who must solve a workplace system hazard?
choices: The newest worker alone
The workplace through shared responsibilities and proper processes
Only a classmate
No one if the shift is busy
feedback: A new worker should report and act safely, not carry the system alone.
Yes. Roles differ, but safety work is shared.
A classmate may support but does not replace the workplace process.
Schedule pressure does not remove the hazard.

practice.prompt: A wage discrepancy needs which first record?
choices: A screenshot of a rumour
A public accusation
Pay period, hours, rate and statement
An unrelated safety poster
feedback: A rumour does not establish this worker’s pay.
Public accusation risks privacy and skips verification.
Yes. These details permit a focused payroll question.
Safety material will not reconcile the pay calculation.

practice.prompt: A worker reports an unpaid hour. What record is the most useful starting point?
choices: The time record and pay statement for the same period.
A photo of unrelated equipment.
A public post naming a coworker.
A safety data sheet for a cleaner.
feedback: Correct: compare records that show the hours and pay in question.
This does not address the pay discrepancy.
Public accusations do not establish the recorded hour and can expose private information.
A chemical document is unrelated to wages.

practice.prompt: A hazard report receives no response and the danger remains. What should the worker do?
choices: Treat silence as proof the risk is fixed.
Use the next appropriate workplace or official safety escalation route.
Resume the task to avoid inconvenience.
Delete the report.
feedback: Silence does not show the hazard was controlled.
Correct: an unresolved risk calls for the next safe reporting step.
Convenience does not make a hazard safe.
Keeping records can help a follow-up.

practice.prompt: Which report is easiest for a supervisor to act on?
choices: “The place is unsafe.”
“At 4 p.m. the guard shifted during the check; I stopped the task and need inspection before resuming.”
“Everyone knows the machine is bad.”
“My coworker is careless.”
feedback: This gives little detail or action.
Correct: it identifies time, observed condition, action, and requested response.
General reputation is not a checkable event.
It speculates about motive and does not describe the hazard.

lessons.transfer: A fictional worker finds repeated missed breaks in their time record. Draft a factual question and choose which current Alberta guidance to check, noting what facts are still missing.
lessons.evidence: Write a short documented concern and a two-step help route for a fictional workplace issue; identify the correct source category.

lessons.title: Recognize discrimination and seek help
lessons.goal: Distinguish an observable workplace event from an assumption, preserve relevant evidence and select a safe help route.
lessons.opening: A supervisor repeatedly assigns training opportunities to some workers but tells another worker, ‘People like you do not do that task.’ What needs to be documented before drawing a conclusion?

teach.heading: Observe before labelling
teach.body: Discrimination concerns involve treatment connected to protected grounds under applicable human-rights law. A worker’s experience matters, but a course scenario cannot determine the legal outcome from one sentence alone. Record the actual words, dates, context, decision made, comparison with relevant opportunities and any witnesses or messages. Avoid speculating about motives as if they were proven facts.

teach.heading: Protect privacy and safety
teach.body: Keep records in a private, appropriate place and avoid posting allegations or other workers’ identities online. Ask a trusted adult, school contact, workplace human-resources contact or representative for support. Where internal steps are unsuitable or do not resolve the issue, consult the current Alberta Human Rights Commission guidance for options and time limits. The right help route depends on the issue and the worker’s circumstances.

teach.heading: Choose an actionable next step
teach.body: A useful request states the event and desired clarification: ‘On Tuesday I was told I could not join the training. What criteria are being used, and how can I apply?’ The response can be compared with the documented pattern. The learner’s task is not to adjudicate a real classmate’s case; use the fictional record to practise evidence, respectful communication and seeking qualified help.

teach.heading: Record facts without exposing others
teach.body: When documenting a concerning incident, keep an exact note of what was said or done, when and where it happened, who was present, and what decision followed. Separate a direct quotation from your interpretation. Preserve relevant messages privately and avoid forwarding them to classmates or posting names. A comparison can be useful, but only if it is fair: compare similar roles, qualifications, timing, and circumstances rather than assuming different outcomes have the same cause.

teach.heading: Seek a suitable and timely help route
teach.body: A trusted adult, school contact, workplace representative, or human-resources contact can help a young worker understand options. If the concern may involve a protected ground or a missed deadline, consult current Alberta Human Rights Commission information promptly because processes and time limits matter. An initial conversation can ask for criteria or clarification without forcing a learner to decide the legal label alone. In class, use the fictional file; do not submit a real allegation, another person’s identity, or confidential employment records. The learner does not have to confront the person alone. Preserve a copy of relevant information, note any immediate safety concern, and choose support before taking a step that feels unsafe.

lessons.title: Show what you can do at work
lessons.goal: Translate a task example into a truthful employability-skill statement for a fictional application.
lessons.opening: A fictional community library hub posts a part-time help-desk role. Rowan has never held a paid job but has helped organize a school event. Can that experience count as evidence?

teach.heading: Skills are shown through actions
teach.body: Employability skills such as communication, problem solving, reliability and collaboration appear in paid and unpaid settings. A first job application does not need to invent employment. Instead, connect a real or fictional task to an action and outcome: what was needed, what the learner did, and what changed. ‘Organized an event’ is a start; ‘kept a sign-up list, confirmed volunteers, and solved a scheduling conflict’ shows what the person can do.

teach.heading: Read the role before writing
teach.body: A useful application responds to actual duties. The library hub needs people who can welcome visitors, keep simple records, protect private information and ask for help when unsure. Rowan should select evidence for those tasks. A long list of personality claims is weaker than two specific examples tied to the posting. Do not overstate a role, claim a credential not held, or share another person’s private information in an example.

teach.heading: Improve with a test
teach.body: Read a skill sentence as if you were the employer: can you picture the action, and could you ask a follow-up question about it? If not, revise. A good first résumé or portfolio can include school projects, service, family responsibilities or personal projects when described appropriately. The course uses a fictional posting so every learner can practise without needing a real employer, résumé history or personal disclosure.

teach.heading: Translate experience into employer evidence
teach.body: A posting describes needs; an application should help the reader find matching evidence quickly. Choose a skill the role actually uses, then give one example with an action and result. A student who helped with a school fundraiser might describe how they checked the count against a list, spotted a mismatch, and asked the coordinator before changing the record. That example shows care and judgement without claiming paid office experience. Keep the example truthful and remove any names or private details about other people.

teach.heading: Make the evidence easy to verify
teach.body: Use specific verbs—checked, sorted, explained, repaired, planned—and avoid unsupported adjectives such as “perfect” or “expert.” If the result is not numeric, describe what changed or what feedback you received. A portfolio item can include a short reflection that names a challenge and what you would do next time. If the learner has no matching example yet, identify a safe practice task they can do in class rather than inventing experience or volunteering for an unsafe task. Use the same care when describing unpaid responsibilities: state the context and avoid suggesting that a project was a formal job. A clear boundary increases trust in the rest of the example.
