lessons.title: Make decisions on a first shift
lessons.goal: Use supplied onboarding information to prepare for a safe, respectful simulated first shift.
lessons.opening: Rowan receives a first-shift note from Prairie Library Hub. It lists a start time and three tasks but does not explain who authorizes access to visitor records. What should Rowan do first?

teach.heading: Read instructions as a system
teach.body: A first-shift message should tell a worker where to arrive, who supervises, what tasks are allowed, what training is required and how to report a problem. If a piece is missing, asking before acting is part of preparation. Do not treat an access code or a casual co-worker suggestion as permission to view private records. A new worker can be reliable while saying, ‘I need the approved procedure before I do that.’

teach.heading: Plan for uncertainty
teach.body: Separate routine questions from urgent hazards. A missing visitor-sign-in instruction calls for a supervisor question; a spill across an exit may require pausing access and using the site’s safety procedure immediately. List the task, missing information, possible consequence and safe interim action. This prepares Rowan to make a good decision even when the exact case differs from the opening note.

teach.heading: Keep the learning online
teach.body: You will use supplied messages, schedules and records in a simulated workday. Read them closely, choose actions and explain why. The case lets you practise preparation, communication and safe judgement without arranging an external placement or disclosing your real employment history. The teacher can assess the reasoning in your written case file; the fictional supervisor in the story provides the feedback needed for later lessons.

teach.heading: Use permission and privacy boundaries
teach.body: Workplace readiness includes knowing what you are authorized to do. A visitor asking for another person’s reservation, phone number, or schedule does not create permission to disclose it. Confirm the site’s identity-check and privacy procedure with the supervisor. If the procedure is missing, explain the request and ask for direction while avoiding confirmation that the record exists. The same principle applies in a simulated course: analyze only the fictional information provided and do not enter real names or records.

teach.heading: Match the response to urgency
teach.body: Classify a situation by immediate danger, privacy, deadline, and your authority. A spill blocking an exit needs an immediate safe action: warn others if safe, keep clear, and use the site emergency process. A printer delay usually needs a clear supervisor update and a proposed workaround. A learner should not improvise with unfamiliar equipment or chemicals. Tell the lead what is known, what is uncertain, what has already been done, and what decision is needed. If the supervisor is unavailable, follow the site’s escalation or emergency directions rather than guessing. The correct action depends on the urgency and the training already provided.

lessons.title: Practise a truthful interview
lessons.goal: Build and revise an interview answer using a situation, action, result and relevant learning.
lessons.opening: The fictional shift lead asks Rowan, ‘Tell me about a time you handled an unexpected change.’ Rowan has an example from a school event, but their first answer is, ‘I am good under pressure.’ How can it improve?

teach.heading: Answer with a small true story
teach.body: An interview answer is stronger when the listener can see what happened. State the situation briefly, the action you took, the result and what you learned. The story does not need to be dramatic or from paid employment. A school project, household responsibility, volunteer task or fictional practice case can demonstrate a skill if it is described honestly. For a real interview, use your own truthful experience and protect other people’s privacy.

teach.heading: Target the question
teach.body: The question asks about change, so Rowan should explain the original plan, what changed, the choice made and its consequence. ‘I worked hard’ does not tell the interviewer how Rowan adapted. A strong answer might say that a volunteer cancelled, Rowan moved the sign-in table, assigned a replacement, and checked that arrivals were still greeted. The result does not need to be perfect; a useful reflection can name a limitation and a better next step.

teach.heading: Make networking safe and purposeful
teach.body: Researching a role can include reading official profiles, attending school-approved events or asking a known adult about their work. No learner must contact a stranger, disclose private information or conduct a real interview for this lesson. Practise two questions for the fictional shift lead: one about daily tasks and one about support or training. A question should help you evaluate the role, not simply flatter the interviewer.

teach.heading: Match the story to the question asked
teach.body: A concise interview response begins with the question’s focus, not a memorized speech. For a question about change, identify the original plan, the new information, the action, and the result. For a question about a mistake, take responsibility for the part you controlled and explain what you learned, without blaming teammates. Use an example that is true in a real interview; this course’s fictional response is for practice only. Keep other people anonymous unless their details are necessary and authorized.

teach.heading: Turn practice into a conversation
teach.body: After drafting, check whether a listener could understand the context in one sentence and whether the result answers the question. Remove details that do not support the point. Practise aloud or in writing, but do not try to memorize a perfect script; follow-up questions may change the direction. Networking can also be a question-led conversation with a known adult or approved guest. Ask about ordinary tasks, training, and challenging parts. No student must contact strangers or share a personal phone number for course completion. A thoughtful answer can include a lesson learned without turning the response into an apology. Be concise enough to leave room for the interviewer’s follow-up.

lessons.title: Work through a changing shift
lessons.goal: Prioritize tasks, protect private information and respond to feedback in a fully supplied workplace simulation.
lessons.opening: At 10:05 a.m. the fictional hub’s printer stops, a visitor asks for a private reservation record, and the shift lead asks Rowan to set up an 11 a.m. activity. Which action comes first?

teach.heading: Triage by consequence and authority
teach.body: In a busy shift, urgency is not the same as importance. Check immediate safety, deadlines, permissions and who can help. Rowan cannot disclose a visitor’s reservation merely because the person asks confidently. The activity setup has a known deadline; the printer failure may block it, but a safe alternative might exist. A good first response is to protect the record, alert the shift lead about the printer, and propose an achievable setup plan.

teach.heading: Make the decision visible
teach.body: A short update to a supervisor should state the problem, what Rowan has already checked, a suggested next step and the help needed. ‘Everything is broken’ leaves the lead to investigate from scratch. ‘The printer stopped after one page; the 11 a.m. cards are not ready. I can use blank cards if you approve’ gives actionable information. Record what was decided so the next task is clear.

teach.heading: Learn from supplied feedback
teach.body: The fictional shift lead notes that Rowan kept visitor information private and solved the activity setup, but waited too long to report the printer problem. Feedback is evidence about a behaviour in this scenario, not a judgement about Rowan’s worth or entire career. Compare the action with the result, choose one specific improvement, and test it in the next changed case. The complete shift record is in this lesson; no real workplace experience is needed to answer.

teach.heading: Use a simple priority test
teach.body: When several tasks arrive, sort them by safety, privacy, deadline, and dependency. A task involving private records may have a strict permission boundary. An activity setup due soon may be urgent but can sometimes use an approved alternative. Ask what blocks other work and which decisions require supervisor authority. This is not a formula that replaces judgement; it gives a reasoned order and makes uncertainty visible. If safety is immediate, use the site procedure before trying to protect a deadline.

teach.heading: Review what the outcome actually shows
teach.body: A busy shift can produce mixed evidence: a learner may protect confidential information and meet a setup deadline yet report equipment failure too late. Write each observation separately, then identify one behaviour to repeat and one to practise earlier. Avoid “I am bad under pressure,” which turns one case into a permanent identity. A useful next test is concrete: send a short supervisor update as soon as a blocker threatens the deadline, then record whether the new timing helped. When two tasks compete, tell the lead early if one cannot be completed safely or on time. A timely request lets the authorized person reset expectations.

lessons.opening: Rowan enjoyed welcoming visitors but found repeated record updates tiring. The fictional shift lead praised clear explanations and suggested earlier equipment reporting. Does one shift prove which career Rowan should choose?

teach.heading: Read feedback in context
teach.body: Feedback describes a particular performance in a particular setting. Rowan’s clear explanations are evidence for a communication strength, while a late printer report identifies an action to improve. Neither is a permanent label. Compare the feedback with Rowan’s earlier strengths card and the actual tasks in the fictional posting. Look for agreement, tension and what remains unknown after one simulated shift.

teach.heading: Revise one claim at a time
teach.body: A useful revision can keep the same broad interest but change the role or route. Rowan may explore visitor services, teaching support or information design while asking how much repetitive record work each requires. The plan should name the old assumption, the new evidence and the next research or practice task. ‘I am bad at administration’ overstates a preference seen in one case; ‘I want to compare roles with different amounts of record work’ is testable.

teach.heading: Prepare a defensible portfolio
teach.body: Use the supplied posting, first-shift note, task board and lead feedback to make a concise evidence chain: task, action, result, interpretation, revised plan. You can quote or paraphrase the fictional records because they are provided here. You do not need a supervisor signature, real job placement, stranger interview or personal employment details to complete this online case. The teacher can assess how well your interpretation follows the evidence.

teach.heading: Make the evidence chain traceable
teach.body: A portfolio claim should point to a record and explain the link. For example: “I want to explore public-facing work” can cite the fictional shift note where Rowan welcomed visitors, then note that the record also shows the learner needs to practise earlier updates when a tool fails. The next step could be comparing roles with different amounts of visitor contact and record work. A reader should be able to tell which part is observed, which is interpretation, and which is a future question.

teach.heading: Revise the plan without overcorrecting
teach.body: New evidence can change a detail, not necessarily an entire goal. If one task was difficult, ask whether it was a skill gap, lack of instruction, a work-condition mismatch, or simply a one-time problem. Choose a small next test to distinguish those explanations. A useful revision is reversible: research another profile, practise a supervisor update, or compare a second role. The supplied course records are enough to demonstrate this process; no signature or real placement is needed. A portfolio is not a prediction of employability. It is a record of current evidence and next steps, which can be revised as the learner gains more information.

document.title: Fictional shift-lead feedback note
rows: Visitors followed sign-in steps without repeat questions
Compare roles with different amounts of record work
Lead learned of problem at noon
document.note: This is simulated feedback. It describes a specific case, not a verified workplace placement.

worked.prompt: Rowan concludes, ‘I must work at a library.’
steps: The feedback supports communication and careful records, not one exclusive occupation.
Identify related roles using those skills.
Research actual duties and conditions before narrowing the plan.
worked.conclusion: A positive case result is a clue, not a career assignment.

worked.prompt: Rowan concludes, ‘I failed because I reported the printer late.’
steps: The record also shows strengths in privacy and visitor communication.
Isolate the behaviour that can change: timing of the update.
Write a specific next action and test it in a new case.
worked.conclusion: Balanced revision uses all relevant evidence rather than one critical sentence.

practice.prompt: What does the simulated shift evidence support most directly?
choices: Rowan explained procedures clearly in this case
Rowan is guaranteed a library career
Rowan dislikes every office task
A real supervisor verified employment
feedback: Yes. That is the observation recorded in this fictional case.
One case cannot guarantee a career route.
The record is narrower than that claim.
The shift and supervisor are fictional.

practice.prompt: Which revision is testable?
choices: I am a failure
I will compare roles with different amounts of record work
I will never change my plan
Everyone else is better at this
feedback: This is a broad self-judgement, not a plan.
Yes. It names a research comparison that can produce new evidence.
A plan should respond to evidence.
Comparison with others does not interpret the work case.

practice.prompt: What should a portfolio explanation connect?
choices: Only the final job title
Only the most positive feedback
Task, action, result, interpretation and revision
A real account of private work
feedback: A title does not show learning.
Include relevant strengths and growth areas.
Yes. The chain shows why the plan changed.
Personal employment information is unnecessary.

practice.prompt: Which portfolio sentence is easiest to trace to supplied evidence?
choices: “I can work anywhere.”
“The shift record shows I kept visitor details private; I want to compare other roles with similar privacy duties.”
“I am bad at equipment.”
“My future is decided.”
feedback: This claim is too broad to evaluate.
Correct: it links an observed action to a next research question.
One printer problem does not prove inability with equipment.
The course emphasizes revisable plans.

practice.prompt: A learner struggled once with record work. What conclusion is most careful?
choices: All administration careers are unsuitable.
Identify whether the difficulty came from task interest, missing instruction, or a one-time circumstance and test further.
Ignore the evidence permanently.
Change every high-school course immediately.
feedback: One event cannot establish every role’s fit.
Correct: competing explanations lead to a better next step.
Evidence should inform further inquiry.
A large irreversible change is not justified by one event.

practice.prompt: What turns a reflection into useful career evidence?
choices: Task, action, result, interpretation, and a next check.
A supervisor signature only.
A confident prediction.
A long description without links to the source records.
feedback: Correct: the chain lets a reader see how the conclusion follows.
A signature is not the only proof and is not required for this simulation.
Predictions are not evidence.
Length does not replace traceability.

lessons.transfer: A second fictional lead praises Rowan’s accurate records but notes that Rowan avoided asking visitors clarifying questions. Revise the strengths claim and design a new practice task.
lessons.evidence: Submit a simulated experience reflection using the supplied case records, with one strength, one growth action, a revised career hypothesis and a next test.
